title: Deepfakes and fake jobs
takeaway: If anyone on a call or in a job chat asks you to install something, leave and verify them another way.

cards.title: Faces, but no sound
cards.body: A contact you know invites you to a partnership call. You join. Familiar faces appear, smiling. But there is no sound. A box pops up asking you to install an update to fix your audio.

lines.label: Greeting
lines.why: A greeting is not the problem.

lines.t: No audio? Install the fix below.
lines.label: Install request on a call
lines.why: Real calls never need a file to fix audio.

cards.title: This happened to real founders
cards.body: In April 2025, Manta Network cofounder Kenny Li joined a call from a known contact. He saw real looking faces, heard nothing, and was asked to download a script to fix audio. He left. In May 2025, Polygon cofounder Sandeep Nailwal warned that fake calls using his face pushed people to install an SDK.
points: Known contacts can be hacked accounts.

cards.title: Fake jobs, real malware
cards.body: Fake recruiters post crypto jobs, move fast, then ask you to download their meeting app or run a code test. The file installs malware that can steal saved logins, browser data and wallets. Researchers link many of these campaigns to North Korean groups.
points: Never run a file or code a stranger sends.
Verify the company through channels you find yourself.

cards.title: If you already installed it
cards.body: Act fast, without shame. Disconnect that device from the internet. From a different, clean device, move your funds to a new wallet and change your passwords. Do not use the infected device for crypto until it is wiped.

cards.title: Try it
cards.body: A recruiter messages you about a job. Tap each red flag, then Done.

seg.label: Compliment
seg.why: A compliment is not the problem.

questions.stem: On a call the faces look real, but the sound fails. They send an audio fix file. What do you do?
options: Leave and verify them another way
Install it, the faces are real
Install it, then scan later
Ask them to resend it as a link
questions.why: Kenny Li faced exactly this in 2025 and left. Real calls never need you to install a file.

questions.stem: Tap every red flag, then Done.

lines.label: Greeting
lines.why: A greeting is not the problem.

lines.label: Fake update claim
lines.why: A caller cannot know your app needs updating.

lines.t: Install the SDK to see our demo.
lines.label: Install request
lines.why: Installing on a call is how malware spreads.

questions.why: A caller pushed an update and an SDK install. Leave the call and verify the person on a channel you find yourself.

questions.stem: A recruiter insists the interview happens on their own meeting app, not one you use. What do you do?
options: Ask for a tool you use, or leave
Install their app, but on a spare laptop
Install it, real recruiters often have custom tools
Install it on your phone, not your laptop
questions.why: A required download instead of common video tools is a known red flag in fake job scams.

questions.stem: During a partnership call, the host asks you to install an SDK to view the demo. What do you do?
options: Refuse, leave and verify them separately
Install it, partners need demos
Install it, the host's face is familiar
Install it on a friend's device
questions.why: Fake calls using a real founder's face pushed SDK installs in 2025. Never install software during an unexpected call.

questions.stem: Tap every red flag, then Done.

seg.label: Greeting
seg.why: A greeting is not the problem.

seg.label: Too good offer
seg.why: Real jobs do not skip every check.

seg.label: Run unknown code
seg.why: Unknown code can steal your wallets.

seg.label: Unknown code site
seg.why: You cannot check what this code does.

questions.why: A too good offer plus code to run from an unknown site is the fake job pattern. Do not run it.

questions.stem: Someone who looks like a famous founder messages you offering a private call. How do you check?
options: Contact them through their official account you found
Trust them if the profile photo matches
Trust them if they know your name
Join the call, but keep your camera off
questions.why: Faces and names can be faked. Verify through an official account you found yourself, not the one that messaged you.

questions.stem: You ran a stranger's update file an hour ago and now feel worried. What do you do first?
options: Disconnect that computer from the internet right away
Wait an hour to see if anything goes missing
Move funds now, using that same computer
Run an antivirus scan, then carry on as normal
questions.why: Disconnect that computer from the internet first. Then use a clean device to move funds to a new wallet and change passwords.

questions.stem: A job test asks you to download their code project and run it on your laptop. You cannot verify the company. What do you do?
options: Do not run it, verify the company first
Run it on the laptop with your wallet
Run it, code tests are normal in hiring
Run it but close your wallet app first
questions.why: Running code from unknown recruiters is how many fake job attacks install malware. Verify the company first, or do not run it.

questions.stem: Tap every red flag, then Done.

lines.label: Greeting
lines.why: A greeting is not the problem.

lines.label: Staged audio problem
lines.why: Fake calls stage audio trouble on purpose.

lines.t: Run this script to fix it.
lines.label: Script to run
lines.why: A script from a caller can take your wallet.

questions.why: A staged audio problem and a script to fix it is the same trick used on Kenny Li in 2025. Leave the call.

questions.stem: A contact you have chatted with for months sends a call invite on Telegram. Can you install whatever the call asks?
options: No, never install anything on a call
Yes, you know this person
Yes, if the faces look right
Yes, if it is a short file
questions.why: In the Manta case the invite came from a known contact. Accounts get hacked, so never install anything a call asks for.
